rows.original: Present Kiyoko with the ring, and ask for her hand in marriage.
rows.translation: 把戒指交给清子，向她求婚吧。
rows.raw: "Present Kiyoko with the ring, and ask for her hand in marriage."

rows.original: No matter how many times you look at her, she only grows more beautiful with each passing day... and kit.
rows.translation: 无论你看她多少次，她都会一天比一天更美丽……还有她肚子里的小狐狸也是一样。
rows.raw: "No matter how many times you look at her, she only grows more beautiful with each passing day... and kit."

rows.original: Even after all this time and everything you've been through together, it's important to connect with each other.
rows.translation: 即使经过了这么长的时间，也经历了那么多共同的事情，彼此之间的沟通与联系仍然非常重要。
rows.raw: "Even after all this time and everything you've been through together, it's important to connect with each other."

rows.translation: 将清子从你的队伍中移除。

rows.original: Ask Kiyoko to accompany you in your adventures.
rows.translation: 邀请清子与你一起踏上冒险之旅吧。
rows.raw: "Ask Kiyoko to accompany you in your adventures."

rows.original: You currently don't have space to take on another party member.
rows.translation: 你目前没有空间来接纳另一位队友了。
rows.raw: "You currently don't have space to take on another party member."

rows.original: Sample some of Kiyoko's traditional cooking.
rows.translation: 尝尝清子的传统料理吧。
你已经和清子一起吃过饭了。

rows.original: Play with your fox-wife. She can be so childish at times...
rows.translation: 和你的狐狸妻子一起玩吧。她有时候真的会像个孩子一样……
rows.raw: "Play with your fox-wife. She can be so childish at times... "

rows.original: You don't need to do this any more... which means that you're doing this because you want to. And that is the most beautiful feeling of all.
rows.translation: 你不再需要这样做……这意味着你这样做是出于自己的意愿。而这种感觉，才是最美好的。
rows.raw: "You don't need to do this any more... which means that you're doing this because you want to. And that is the most beautiful feeling of all."

rows.original: Saying nothing, you pick up your porcelain cup of tea and sip it gently as you let your gaze roam over Kiyoko's face. Realizing what you're doing, your beloved fox-wife lowers her eyes for a second or two before raising them to meet yours, unconsciously toying with one of the twin amber locks of hair that frame her face, rubbing the silken, glossy hair between thumb and forefinger before twirling it about the latter. "If you're going to stare at me, I'm going to stare right back at you," she says, a small, playful smile on her lips. That's okay. You know that you're positively irresistible. That gets her truly laughing in that lilting, flute-like voice of hers, giving you an opening to study your lovely kitsune wife in earnest. Framed by twin locks of amber hair, Kiyoko's face is soft and rounded, her chin a gentle point beneath her lips, her large eyes a soothing shade of sea-green jade. In place of human ears are two large fox ears that sit atop her head, each one easily larger than your hand. As you watch, they wiggle, twitch and swivel with a life of their own, refusing to fall in line with Kiyoko's calm demeanour. Each of their insides is a clean white to contrast with her amber coloration, and filled with large, fluffy and ever-so-sensitive tufts of fur; it's very, very hard to not want to reach out and start petting them. With the way her pregnancies are filling out her hips and ass, now quite wide and very definitely grabbable even through her skirts, she looks every bit the role of the calm and wise matron of her brood. It's not just one or two spots, but her overall figure — she hasn't gotten any taller or anything like that, but Kiyoko looks sturdier, healthier, her body more able to provide the requisite underlying framework that's necessary to support such prodigious fecundity. She's not quite voluptuous yet, but rapidly approaching that point. |After having birthed so many little fox kits, Kiyoko's body laughs at the idea that the process might be anything more than a minor inconvenience. With those blatant hips of hers, clearly visible even under her skirts, one can easily envision kit after kit slipping out of her tummy and into the world without any trouble at all. Her butt is so round and plush you could probably use it as a pillow, and coupled with her fluffy tails, that actually sounds like an idea you could get behind. Not that being a fox factory has harmed her any. When she's not pregnant, Kiyoko's figure defaults to a gentle hourglass shape, all the better to advertise her terminal case of baby rabies with. |By now, you're pretty sure that Kiyoko could start a fertility cult all by herself if she wanted to. Your kitsune slut-wife takes positive delight in showing off her kit-bearing hips to you, giving them a suggestive waggle in your direction while you look on. With assets like these, added to an expansive but still firm ass? She'd spit out children with the same ease other women spit out watermelon seeds. At this point, she'd barely even feel it. "Oh come on, there's no need to be shy. You made me like this, after all." If she insists. Even her thigh gap has widened to the point where she's had to adjust her stance yet again, but Kiyoko doesn't seem to regret any moment of this — quite the opposite, in fact. After all this time, Kiyoko is now practically the spitting image of the idealised den mother; even if she wanted to — and you know full well she does — you don't think she can appear more maternal than she is already. ] Finally, you move onto Kiyoko's midriff, just under her sash. [kiyoko.pregStage 0 1 2 3 4 |Your kitsune wife's slender torso belies her vulpine grace, softly feminine as it curves in from her chest and outwards as it approaches her hips. Accentuated by her sash, just looking at her trim body gives you an impression of dainty yet lithe alacrity; while Kiyoko usually gets about in deliberate, measured movements, there's no doubt that she could rapidly pick up her pace if the situation called for it. [kiyoko.numKits 2 |Despite her having had a number of children, your kitsune slut-wife's tummy is as it always has been. Pregnancies tend to wear other women out, especially when they come as often as they do for Kiyoko, but clearly things are very, very different when it comes to kitsune destined to be den mothers. ] |A gentle swell pushes against the fabric of her yukata, forming a slight bump that marks the uh, essence that she's received from you and is nurturing in her body. Maybe it's because she's a spirit, or maybe she's just got that much willpower, but Kiyoko appears completely unfazed by the usual complaints which accompany the early stages of pregnancy. "It's still quite soon; this one's still so little," Kiyoko says, folding her ears forward and clasping her hands together over her bump with a smile. "I've no doubt I'll be getting much, much bigger before I'm done, though." You feel the same way. It hasn't been that long, and she's already visibly showing through her clothes. |Your kitsune wife's belly is growing nicely, already of considerable heft and size — perhaps somewhat more than what one might expect at this stage of her pregnancy. It's enough for Kiyoko's tummy to bulge out of her clothing, requiring her to hike up her sash as it pulls the fabric of her yukata off her shoulders. One's got to admit that it does make Kiyoko look more attractive and maternal... perhaps she could do with a little more of your chi. Noticing you staring at her, Kiyoko lowers her eyes demurely, then raises her gaze to your with a sly grin. Clearly reading the thoughts off your face like words off a page, your fox-wife slowly licks her lips even as a slight blush creeps into her face. "I'm being a very good mother to your kits, aren't I? As repayment... well, you can play with me lots soon, if you know what I mean. It can get quite droll when you're not around." Maybe later. For now, you want to give her a proper inspection. "If that's what you want..." Barely has she said the words before she disrobes partially, thrusting the pale rise of her increasingly pregnant belly at you. It looks even more swollen exposed like this, a full, hard curve jutting out from her midriff, and Kiyoko looks absolutely proud of her condition as you note that her tummy button is dangerously close to popping outwards. All right, that's enough. She can put her things back on now. |With how full and ripe her belly is, the moment of birthing can't be too far away. Noticing you watching her, Kiyoko runs a hand across the gravid mound of her pregnancy, sighing softly as she feels the kitsune kit within kick. Smooth, hard and round, there's no mistaking the fecund shape of Kiyoko's increasingly stuffed womb as it presses tightly against the silky fabric of her yukata. Burdened with the weight of the kit rapidly growing inside her and impending birth, her tummy has begun to drop, slowly shifting into a position more conducive to birthing even as her navel has finally popped out. [kiyoko.numKits 8 |To make things even better, a rosy patch has begun to spread out over the stretched skin of Kiyoko's belly, a telltale sign of the attention her body's giving to her womb now that she's becoming ever more of a fox factory. ] "You know, even though all this started in a bid for me to get out of my prison... and even now that that's over with, I can't even imagine wanting to stop. It doesn't just feel good on the outside, but on the inside as well... I really, really enjoy being a mother and being with child, even if it has its less desirable moments." |Seems like Kiyoko's pregnancy is in its final stages. Her belly looks fit to be somewhere about eleven or even twelve months pregnant on a normal woman, sticking out quite a ways from her; she no longer ties her sash about her back, but rather in front where she can reach it, snuggling the bow in the valley between the mound of her pregnancy and her milk-laden breasts. The added weight's forced her to start walking with a pronounced waddle and her womb is hanging low in front of her; whenever her hands aren't occupied, they're cradled under her immense pregnancy for what support they can give. Her tummy button has popped out even further to the point where you can see it under her clothing, a marker of how obscenely — and pleasurably — gravid she is. There's no doubt that the kit is rapidly running out of space in an increasingly overstuffed womb, pushing against its mother's hips as it waits to be born. Kiyoko's had to make a few adjustments to her yukata to turn it into appropriate maternity wear, and you have to say it fits her very well — there's a good contrast with her amazingly glossy hair and fur. The big belly coupled with her sometimes playful, sometimes distant gaze, does make her look extremely attractive in a picture of maternal glory. "I have to admit, being like this can be quite distressing at times. I'll just look up from the laundry or wake up from a nap and want to play, but there's no one to play with... it sounds silly, but being so heavy makes me so frisky to boot." Ha! [kiyoko.numKits 8|To wrap it all up, the rosy patch on Kiyoko's pregnant belly has grown to encompass most of it, deepening to a bright red in the process to stand out in stark contrast with her pale skin. If there's any proof that your kitsune slut-wife is the best fox-factory around, this is it. ] ] Your examination of your fox-wife complete, you set down your tea and give Kiyoko a satisfied nod. In return, she dips her head ever so slightly at you, large, fluffy ears twitching, and gives you a small grin. "If we're done admiring each other, let's move on." Gladly. Although you might want to ask — exactly what's it about you that she was admiring? Kiyoko smirks and shakes her head. "Wouldn't be fun if I just up and told you, would it? I'll leave that one for you to figure out on your own." "

rows.original: Kiyoko perks up at the suggestion, her [kiyoko.kiyokoTails] tails curling about herself. [party.has kiyoko |[rand |"It is nice to be able to sit down in comfortable surroundings and talk without being hurried. Being on the road leaves little time for extended conversation... thank you for doing this." |"Ah, a chance to rest and relax, to take one's mind off the worries of travel. Please, beloved, choose a topic to your liking. Here we can discuss matters of a lengthier or more private nature." |"The perils of travel make lengthy conversation impossible, and certain subjects are dangerous to discuss out in the wild. Here, though, we can relax and take our time. We have all night if need be..." ] |[rand |"You wish to talk? So do I. The sound of another person's voice is something you take for granted, until you no longer hear it. After having been through all this, I have learned to treasure the joy of simple conversation." |"Enjoying a pleasant conversation with someone whose company you appreciate is a boon to be savoured, especially when you do not know when the person will next visit. Now, did you have a particular topic in mind, beloved?" |"I'd like that very much, thank you. In fact, I would be honored to have a simple conversation with you over tea and sweets." That's pushing it a little, isn't it? "Not when you've learned to appreciate another person's company as keenly as I do. Please, steer the conversation however you wish." ] ]

rows.translation: 和你那位狐狸妻子聊些闲话吧。

rows.translation: 问问清子，她对你其他同伴有什么看法。
rows.raw: "Ask Kiyoko for her opinion of your other companions."

rows.translation: 看看她会对别人说些什么。

rows.original: [var0 |[rand |"Now that things have come to this, I suppose it's time for me to live out the rest of my natural life from where it would have been," your fox-wife says with a smile. "Given the lifespans of my ancestors, I probably have anywhere between a hundred and ten to a hundred and twenty years remaining before I go to join my forebears. I plan to make the most of that time in service of the imperial colonies." [pc.ra kitsune |You're looking forward to spending that time with her, then. "To be able to grow old with the one you love is a treasure that is often undervalued. You've given so much to be with me, even going as far as to... well. I am grateful. Let us hope that we've many peaceful years ahead of us, then." |A hundred and ten to a hundred and twenty, huh... it's a little shocking to realize that Kiyoko will probably outlive you by a handful of decades, if her reckoning is right. You can't help but feel a little sad at the thought. "There cannot be joy without sadness, nor happiness without pain. Parting is the price we pay for the memories we create together." ] |"I hope this peace lasts," Kiyoko says with a wistful sigh. "Things are tense enough to keep people from growing lax, but peaceful enough that there is no true danger. If Komari's boy goes insane for a lack of a war to fight — well, his desires are tragic, but they do not overrule the needs and lives of everyone who lives in the colonies. Perhaps if this continues, we will finally be able to formally reveal ourselves to the natives and have actual, if tense, dealings with them in the open." |"Komari has been looking troubled for a little while now. She says she senses danger in the future, but his divine lordship does not wish to discuss it with her for the time being. He says if it spreads to the colonies, he will let her know, but not to worry for the time being. Naturally, knowing my retainer, this just made her worry more. I wonder if that was his intention." Danger? "Possibly grave, but knowing what we do, I assume it would involve our quest." That doesn't quite match up, though. If Keros said the Marches weren't involved yet, then the troubles he's worried about can't originate with Kasyrra, for obvious reasons. Then... "It's one of those mysteries we'll discover the answer to if the time comes, beloved. No point worrying about it." |"It gives me great pleasure to be able to see the restoration of my former home to something of its past state, even if in a much reduced fashion. After all, we do not need all of the old buildings, and some of them should be rightly condemned and torn down. Still, to see what was left to decay rebuilt with new splendour and hope... it makes me optimistic for our family's future here across the ocean." She can never return home, you take it. "No. It would cause... political difficulties, and those are the least of what would happen. I'm not willing to create such troubles for my own selfish desires. Maybe this can never truly be my home in spirit the way it is for our daughter, but it is my home in body." |"I'm still adjusting to life outside of the Astral Plane. It's better than it used to be, but I still forget that salt and miso aren't going to just appear in the cupboard when I need them, and I have to send [kiyoko.numKits 4 |one of the kits |Kinu ] over to Kohaku's to get some. That sort of thing. "It's all for the better, though. At least now [kiyoko.numKits 4 |the children have |Kinu has ] to pay attention to detail when out about chores. You know that I tried to prepare them for this by not having the Astral Plane do everything for them, but even so, reality is a much harsher teacher than I could even be." She seems to have done all right, though. "That's because you aren't privy to all the small folliables I'm prone to. There are more than enough to keep me on my toes, and when I consciously correct myself on one I become aware of another. They will eventually run out, I suppose, but it may yet be some time before I catch up with the world as it is..." ] |"[rand |Twice this place has come under hostile scrutiny, and twice has it suffered losses," your fox-wife says with a sigh. "But at least this time around, nothing that was irreplaceable was lost. We all still have each other, beloved, and that is the most important thing of all. What was destroyed can be rebuilt, what was stolen can be replaced, but a life taken cannot ever be given back. [kinu.isInari |Our daughter and I may have some disagreements from time to time, vehement ones, perhaps... but at the end of the day, she is still my flesh and blood and I do not wish for her to perish, even if she thinks as much of me |I confess, if I were to lose her[kiyoko.numKits 2 | or any of our children ], I am not entirely sure what I would do. I fully believe our daughter is the kind of prodigy who only surfaces once every few generations, and if her life were to be snuffed out by such cruel happenstance the tragedy would be immense ]." That's one silver lining, yes; that Kinu[kiyoko.numKits 2 3 | and her sister | and her siblings ] are safe... but it's undeniable that she has been wounded, and not necessarily physically. For that, you aren't ever going to forgive her attackers. Kiyoko gives you a weak smile. "I was not asking you to, beloved. Indeed, they must be taught a lesson for daring to harm our daughter... a terrible one at that." |Our firstborn daughter has been very quiet of late," Kiyoko says, her gaze shifting this way and that as she looks a little troubled. "[kinu.isInari |Well, more than usual. She was never quite the one for idle conversation, but after the attempt on her life, she has become outright morose. She spends all her spare time about that big block of a farmer boy these days, practically clinging off him like moss on a tree |Well, for who she is — Kinu has always been so gregarious, and now she is reduced to not much more than making social pleasantries in order not to be impolite. No one says anything, but I think everyone understands that she's not her usual self, and they politely give her some space; she spends all her spare time about Komari's great-great-grandson, the military provost ]." That's not hard to figure out — she probably feels a lot more secure about him than anywhere else right now. It must be hard with the memory fresh in mind, not being able to feel safe in your own home, not being able to rest easy at night. But as the saying goes, time heals all wounds, and hopefully it holds true for Kinu. "She has been throwing herself into her work," Kiyoko replies. "Which is not an incorrect thing to do — there is value in the mind-clearing nature of simple, repetitive tasks, which [kinu.isInari |low-skilled labor such as what she favors certainly falls under |Komari has been kind enough to dole out to her on a daily basis ]. It is our way, and certainly better than lying idle and allowing her mind to wander and dwell upon ugly thoughts and memories." Mm... [kiyoko.numKits 4 | "There is another matter, too. Asagiri has asked for my permission to study to be a shrine maiden under Miko and Mai; this request has been backed up by Komari herself. It would appear that after [kiyoko.numKits 5 |showing considerable bravery in pulling her siblings out of the fire |having had such a harrowing experience ], our little white-furred daughter has experienced a spiritual awakening. If she is to have a religious education, I can think of no better teacher than Komari, be it in the colonies or otherwise." Just... just how bad are Asagiri's burns? Everyone you've asked has danced around the subject. You know that they aren't life-threatening, but... "They are not serious; she was more frightened than actually wounded. In a sense, that is better — she was able to act despite her fear. That is to be lauded." Phew. "Strictly speaking, Mikoto and Miyuki do not need another pair of hands around the shrine, but it would be welcome. That, and the prestige and social regard that comes with it is not inconsiderable, especially in a backwater like the colonies. The white-furred shrine maiden or priestess is the quintessential Kerosite symbol, as it were... if they think of Kinu as some kind of princess, then Asagiri as a shrine maiden... it will give people hope, and that is what they need." You... you see. While you don't know the full ramifications of all of this owing to cultural differences, you trust your fox-wife as the mother of your kits to do what is best for them. That's about the best you can hope for. "Asagiri has become... inflamed. Passionate. She may have been largely unharmed in the physical sense, but something has irrevocably changed in our daughter as a result of the experience. In all of our children." Kiyoko sighs and looks away. "They grow up so fast. Was it but the blink of an eye ago that I was holding Kinu as a newborn kit in my arms?" ... "I'm sorry. But no, you have no objections with our daughter pursuing this path in life?" Well, it sounds like everything was already decided before you even came along — that, and you wouldn't know enough to bring up a reasonable and coherent objection if you had one. Sure if that's what your wispy little daughter has become, then that's what she'll be. ] |When I first chose to settle in this place more than two centuries ago, I did so because it was defensible. The crater walls created a natural bulwark against the outside world, and the entrance hidden by the waterfall grotto and pool made for a secure home — or so I thought, anyway. Fresh water and even a thermal vent welling up from underground, fertile soil and safety." Kiyoko sighs, and a faraway look enters her eyes. "And now what has happened to me almost happened to my daughter. Were I more superstitious, I would consider this place cursed." She can always retreat to Komari's den if worst comes to worst; you know her retainer would be more than happy to receive her and [kiyoko.numKits 1 |Kinu |your children ]. "[kiyoko.numKits 8 |The arcology may look impressively large from the outside, but much of the space within the living tree is meant for purposes other than living quarters. When one needs to maintain the potential to be completely self-contained at a moment's notice, room that is not being utilised in some fashion is hard to come by. Furthermore, even the poor in the Old Country are expected to live with some measure of dignity, no matter how destitute. Being packed together like sardines on a skewer is no way to live, even in a frontier prospecting camp, and the seat of the colonial governor is anything but. People must have space and room, and with a family as large as ours imposing on her is simply out of the question. "Furthermore, h |No. H ]is divine lordship was kind enough to restore part of the den for me, and tasked me and my issue with finishing the task for him. Abandoning a task directly issued by divinity is out of the question. I will not give up; I will complete the task I started more than two centuries ago and either found a home here or die trying. I cannot just keep on living off my retainer indefinitely." |It is a strange feeling, knowing that your children have been attacked, and yet almost successfully having escaped from the raid on their own. Given such overwhelming odds, one might have expected them to certainly perish, as opposed to hold out for long enough for help to arrive. I feel sad that they have had to grow up so fast — seeing [kiyoko.numKits 2 3 4 |Kinu and Aya |Kinu, Aya and Tatsumi |Kinu, Aya, Tatsumi and Asagiri |Kinu ] changed so profoundly makes the heart ache. Yet there is a sense of pride in understanding their accomplishments and willingness to survive despite the odds. Ah, how it makes the heart ache." Oh, you understand exactly how she feels. It's heartwarming to know that the young have come into their own and proven themselves against real adversity, yet there's the desire to shield them from that adversity just a little longer, let them enjoy their childhood for just a bit more. Kiyoko gives you a small smile, a brief moment of levity in all this. "Being a parent is hard. From start, to middle, to end — never a moment's rest. [kinu.isInari |Well, at least our daughter is putting that independence she so prides herself on to good use, isn't she? |Well, at least we now know our daughter is hiding some good steel beneath that fine silken appearance, isn't she? ]" You chuckle at that. |When I first settled this place, I thought the crater walls would be sufficient natural deterrent and defense to dissuade anyone or anything from making forays into my newly-founded den. That has proven to be insufficient to the determined... I have considered additional defenses, but without enough skilled hands to man them they would be not much better than what is already there. One can only imagine how it must be for the isolated homesteads and prospectors out there in the wilderness; the frontier is a wild, lawless and dangerous place, after all." You've noticed that, yes. Once you get past the gates of Hawkethorne, the Marches are a free-for-all, and moreso after Kasyrra's arrival. Komari herself is understaffed and underequipped when it comes to security, and she's the best the foxen have around... no, to be honest, her people may be more skilled and disciplined than the Hawekthorne militia, less than that of an established power like the Winter City. "It is, like so many other problems, a multi-generational one. Parents must work tirelessly, knowing that they will never live to see the fruits of their efforts; their labors are passed on to their children, who must understand the importance of the task and be ready to receive it without complaint." Kiyoko says with a sigh. ] |[kinu.isInari |[rand |"Please watch out for our daughter while you can, beloved," Kiyoko says with a sigh. "I know that I ought to be in a better position to do so, given than you are out and about [pc.ra kitsune |doing his divine lordship's will |on your adventures ], but she won't listen to me at all. Even if it were to be disadvantageous or even harmful to her, if I told her to do something she would likely do the opposite out of sheer contrariness. If nothing else, at least she will entertain your words." Kinu... is smart, but self-admittedly not very wise. While you have confidence that your daughter is working on that, you can't help but wish that gaining wisdom didn't take so long. "Nor is it evenly distributed. But the point stands — I will do what I can without her knowledge, but please, when you talk to her, maybe you can convince our daughter to be sensible. Even if she believes that I think of her as a mistake, I just... ah, I must have done something terrible in a past life to deserve this kind of dilemma to be placed before me." |"Sometimes, I wonder if it were better that Kinu was not born as talented as she is. Remember? When she was a kit, I used to say that she came out of the womb old and reciting poetry. Now, she thinks herself so talented as to be independent and able to do so much under her own power. "If only she realizes just how many people are looking out for her and everything she has was built by others, you and me included. But it's hard to understand that you're standing on the shoulders of others when you're enjoying the view from up there." If she had to work a little more for what she has, she would have a greater appreciation for its value, you agree. Too much, too soon — now that she's a young woman, you can see how being so talented can be a hindrance. "Even after what happened to her the first time, she's just so reluctant to accept help, like always. The girl believes she can overcome this by herself, because — it just exasperates me at times. Her life is not her own to throw away, not when so many other people have pinned their hopes on her. To say that it is irresponsible is but an understatement." |How's Kinu hanging on? "Our daughter rarely talks to me these days outside of matters pertaining to the management of our household," Kiyoko admits with a sigh. Your fox-wife curls her [kiyoko.kiyokoTails] about herself and folds her hands, her expression carefully and politely inscrutable in the manner of kitsune when they're trying to hide their real emotions. "But she is as always, as far as I can tell; she sleeps soundly at night, has a very good appetite and certainly has not stopped tending to the fields, both here at home and over at Komari's. Our daughter is as predictable as a stone in that regard." She's certainly not afraid of expressing her thoughts and opinions, so if she's out of sorts you're sure she'll let someone know, even if it's not Kiyoko or you. "On the other hand, she's also too stiff-necked to accept help from other people even when she sorely needs it; one can only wonder which aspect of our dearest daughter's personality will win out in the end. [kiyoko.numKits 2 3 |Our other daughter turned out so well; |All our other children turned out so well; ]I just don't know where I went wrong in raising her." |You know that Kinu herself has been targeted, but aside from that [kiyoko.numKits 2 3 |is Aya in danger, too |are her siblings in danger, too |has anyone else close to her been placed in danger, too ]? |你们俩有没有什么办法可以帮助小娟呢？你们经常外出，她也是同样的情况。[party.has kiyoko |始终在你身边 ]我和小毬正在研究我们掌握的为数不多的线索，但如果那些凶手的目标是来自‘道路之间’的人的话——嗯，那个存在领域实在是广阔得难以想象。就像我家乡那些被森林覆盖的山脉一样……很多人进入那里后就再也消失了。 不过可以肯定的是，这些……人拥有我从未见过的支持力量。这种力量无疑是超自然的，而且非常强大。” 在小娟的故事中，那个名叫拉斐尔的人提到了一个名叫陶思的领主。 我知道，而且我们在任何地方都找不到关于那个名字的任何记载。它就好像是在某个时刻凭空出现的一样，而考虑到他的追随者们所拥有的那些力量，这一点实在值得怀疑。像这样的存在，早就应该被那些有权势的人注意到了才对。" 目前，主要的障碍在于你对女儿的敌人了解得太少——要是你知道该从哪里开始寻找信息该多好。 “证据确实很少，亲爱的，但我和科马里正在尽我们所能利用现有的线索。我们已经想出了一些获取更多信息的方法……不过，利用我们的女儿作为诱饵这个办法让我很不满。我们还没有到那么绝望的地步。 ] ] ]

"Given the lifespans of my ancestors, I probably have anywhere between a hundred and ten to a hundred and twenty years remaining before I go to join my forebears. "To be able to grow old with the one you love is a treasure that is often undervalued. You've given so much to be with me, even going as far as to... well. I am grateful. "Things are tense enough to keep people from growing lax, but peaceful enough that there is no true danger. He says if it spreads to the colonies, he will let her know, but not to worry for the time being. Naturally, knowing my retainer, this just made her worry more. I wonder if that was his intention." Danger? "Possibly grave, but knowing what we do, I assume it would involve our quest." That doesn't quite match up, though. If Keros said the Marches weren't involved yet, then the troubles he's worried about can't originate with Kasyrra, for obvious reasons. Then... "It's one of those mysteries we'll discover the answer to if the time comes, beloved. No point worrying about it." |"It gives me great pleasure to be able to see the restoration of my former home to something of its past state, even if in a much reduced fashion. After all, we do not need all of the old buildings, and some of them should be rightly condemned and torn down. Still, to see what was left to decay rebuilt with new splendour and hope... it makes me optimistic for our family's future here across the ocean." She can never return home, you take it. "No. It would cause... political difficulties, and those are the least of what would happen. I'm not willing to create such troubles for my own selfish desires. Maybe this can never truly be my home in spirit the way it is for our daughter, but it is my home in body." |"I'm still adjusting to life outside of the Astral Plane. It's better than it used to be, but I still forget that salt and miso aren't going to just appear in the cupboard when I need them, and I have to send [kiyoko.numKits 4 |one of the kits |Kinu ] over to Kohaku's to get some. That sort of thing. "It's all for the better, though. At least now [kiyoko.numKits 4 |the children have |Kinu has ] to pay attention to detail when out about chores. You know that I tried to prepare them for this by not having the Astral Plane do everything for them, but even so, reality is a much harsher teacher than I could even be." She seems to have done all right, though. "That's because you aren't privy to all the small folliables I'm prone to. There are more than enough to keep me on my toes, and when I consciously correct myself on one I become aware of another. They will eventually run out, I suppose, but it may yet be some time before I catch up with the world as it is..." ] |"[rand |Twice this place has come under hostile scrutiny, and twice has it suffered losses," your fox-wife says with a sigh. What was destroyed can be rebuilt, what was stolen can be replaced, but a life taken cannot ever be given back. [kinu.isInari |Our daughter and I may have some disagreements from time to time, vehement ones, perhaps... but at the end of the day, she is still my flesh and blood and I do not wish for her to perish, even if she thinks as much of me |I confess, if I were to lose her[kiyoko.numKits 2 | or any of our children ], I am not entirely sure what I would do. That's not hard to figure out — she probably feels a lot more secure about him than anywhere else right now. It must be hard with the memory fresh in mind, not being able to feel safe in your own home, not being able to rest easy at night. But as the saying goes, time heals all wounds, and hopefully it holds true for Kinu. "She has been throwing herself into her work," Kiyoko replies. Everyone you've asked has danced around the subject. You know that they aren't life-threatening, but... "They are not serious; she was more frightened than actually wounded. In a sense, that is better — she was able to act despite her fear. That is to be lauded." Phew. "Strictly speaking, Mikoto and Miyuki do not need another pair of hands around the shrine, but it would be welcome. You... you see. While you don't know the full ramifications of all of this owing to cultural differences, you trust your fox-wife as the mother of your kits to do what is best for them. That's about the best you can hope for. "Asagiri has become... inflamed. Passionate. "They grow up so fast. Was it but the blink of an eye ago that I was holding Kinu as a newborn kit in my arms?" ... "I'm sorry. But no, you have no objections with our daughter pursuing this path in life?" Well, it sounds like everything was already decided before you even came along — that, and you wouldn't know enough to bring up a reasonable and coherent objection if you had one. Sure if that's what your wispy little daughter has become, then that's what she'll be. ] |When I first chose to settle in this place more than two centuries ago, I did so because it was defensible. Fresh water and even a thermal vent welling up from underground, fertile soil and safety." Kiyoko sighs, and a faraway look enters her eyes. "And now what has happened to me almost happened to my daughter. Were I more superstitious, I would consider this place cursed." She can always retreat to Komari's den if worst comes to worst; you know her retainer would be more than happy to receive her and [kiyoko.numKits 1 |Kinu |your children ]. It's heartwarming to know that the young have come into their own and proven themselves against real adversity, yet there's the desire to shield them from that adversity just a little longer, let them enjoy their childhood for just a bit more. Kiyoko gives you a small smile, a brief moment of levity in all this. "Being a parent is hard. From start, to middle, to end — never a moment's rest. [kinu.isInari |Well, at least our daughter is putting that independence she so prides herself on to good use, isn't she? |Well, at least we now know our daughter is hiding some good steel beneath that fine silken appearance, isn't she? ]" You chuckle at that. |When I first settled this place, I thought the crater walls would be sufficient natural deterrent and defense to dissuade anyone or anything from making forays into my newly-founded den. "It is, like so many other problems, a multi-generational one. Sort of like the forested mountains of my homeland, to be sure... people go in there to disappear. "What is certain, though, is that these... people have backing of a kind that I have never seen before. Certainly supernatural, and strong at that." In Kinu's tale, the man — Raphael — mentioned a Lord Taoth. "I know, and there are no references anywhere to that name that we can find. It's like it materialized out of thin air at some point, which should be suspect for the kind of power his followers appear to have. Something or someone like that should have been noticed the powers that be a long time ago." Right now, the main impediment is how little you actually know of your daughter's enemies — if only you knew where to begin looking. "The evidence is scarce, beloved, but Komari and I are doing all we can with what we have. Several possibilities have come up with regards to acquiring more information... but I am not pleased with the prospect of using our daughter as bait. We are not that desperate yet." ] ] ] '

rows.original: So, can she tell you something of her patron deity? "It wouldn't be right of me to speak of him behind his back," Kiyoko replies, her ears twitching and swivelling this way and that, as if expecting the deity himself to step out of thin air. "However, there are very many well-known fables about his exploits, and learning about what he's reputedly done might give you some insight into my master. Would you like to hear one of them?" Well, since you asked the question, there can't be any harm in it, can there? Kiyoko nods, moistens her throat with a sip of tea, and begins.
rows.translation: 那么，她能跟你讲讲她的守护神吗？ “我背着他谈论他，这样做是不妥的。”清子回答道，她的耳朵不停地抽动着，来回转动着，仿佛期待着那位神明真的会从空气中出现一样。“然而，关于他的种种事迹，有许多广为流传的寓言故事。了解那些关于他的传说，或许能帮助你更好地理解我的主人。你想听其中一个故事吗？” 嗯，既然你提出了这个问题，那么问出来也没什么坏处吧？ 清子点了点头，喝了一口茶润了润喉咙，然后开始讲述起来。

rows.original: [rand|The Sultan, ruler of Jassira, was proud and thought himself the cleverest man in the realm. It was true that he was extremely learned, and a man such as he enjoyed calling scholars from all over Savarra to ask them questions none could answer. What fun it was to flaunt his wit and shame others as he did! "Where is the center of the world?" the Sultan would ask, and then laugh when none could reply. Of course, he himself did not know the answer, but by his asking of the question, everyone assumed that he knew it — or was too cowed by his station to suggest otherwise. So happy was he with his scheme that he issued a proclamation: "The one who can tell me where the center of the world is shall receive all the wealth of Jassira. However, answer wrongly and you will receive only death." Who didn't want a fortune? Yet few were willing to risk execution to meet the Sultan's challenge — up until the day a strange, spindly catfolk dressed in motley yellow came up to the Sultan's palace. "I wish to meet the Sultan's challenge," he said. This was something which none had dared before, and soon the entire court had gathered while the catfolk was brought in his rags before the Sultan. "So, you wish to answer my riddle? Know that if your answer is wrong, then death awaits you." "I know this." "Very well. Where is the center of the world?" The stranger gave a sly grin before the Sultan's court, making sure all the noble lords and ladies of the catfolk had their eyes on him. "Why, right under my feet. It goes wherever I go, oh Sultan; as I move, so does the center of the world." "That's insane!" the Sultan exclaimed. "Is it? Well, oh great Sultan, if I'm wrong, bring us the world and we shall measure it together. Surely a lowly commoner like me can be easily proven wrong." The Sultan sputtered, the Sultan grumbled. Here was someone who had called his bluff! Yet he was not about to give a fortune to a mere man in rags! "That riddle was just the first. Here is another one: how many stars are in the sky?" "Neither too many nor too few," the stranger answered calmly. "That's not an answer!" the Sultan roared. "It's not? Then we shall go up together to the heavens and count the stars, oh Sultan. Then and only then may I be proven wrong." "Ridiculous," the sultan snarled. "Impossible. Very well, vagabond, I lay before you a final question: how many hairs are there on my head?" "As many as there are on my tail," came the reply. "Wrong!" the Sultan cried, leaping up from his jewelled throne and making as if to strangle the stranger where he stood. "That is wrong!" "Ah, but before you can be sure of that, oh wise Sultan, you must first count the hairs on both your hair and on my tail." The Sultan had enough of being made a fool of by this no-name stranger, doubly so in front of his court. With the whispers running through the lords and ladies of the catfolk, he knew that the story would spread — and there was nothing he could do to contain it. But at least he could make an example of this stranger who had dared to shame him this way. "Guards!" the Sultan cried. "Seize this cretin!" Before anyone could lay a hand on the stranger, though, the rags fell away from his body, and the catfolk was now a very vulpine and handsome man. As gasps ran through the court and many sought to prostrate themselves before Keros, the Trickster stepped up to the Sultan and gave the lord of the catfolk a mocking bow. "You think yourself clever, oh Sultan, and indeed you are so. But always remember that there are always those more clever than you." With a laugh, the Trickster vanished from sight, but that was not the last of it. When the Sultan later checked on his treasury, it had been utterly and completely emptied of all the wealth of Jassira. |Keros was minding his own peaceful business one day, walking through the streets of the capital in his favorite guise of an amber-furred catfolk in rags. Suddenly he saw two young men coming his way, and it was clear from their face they were in trouble. "What's wrong?" the Trickster asked, going up to them. "Can I help you?" The young men exchanged worried sighs. One of them looked at his companion, who nodded. "We are in terrible trouble. You see, ten months ago we came to the capital to find work. We were tired and hungry, so much so that we could not go any further, and so we stopped in a restaurant. There we ordered two eggs for each of us, a total of four boiled and pickled ones — but after we had eaten, we discovered we had no money left! To our eternal shame, we were forced to sneak out without paying." The Trickster frowned. "Is that it? Then go back and pay what you owe!" "That's what we did!" the second man exclaimed. "We finally managed to find work, and just the other day we returned to the restaurant and tried to pay the owner the single copper piece we owed him for the eggs. We told him our story, confessed our shame, and wished to make amends." "That sounds like a fair price for four eggs," Keros agreed. "That's the problem! The owner would not take it!" "Oh? Was he rewarding you for your honesty?" "Just the opposite! He claimed that if we'd not eaten the eggs, they'd have become chickens. Those chickens would have laid more eggs, and in these ten months he'd have perhaps thirty or so chickens from those selfsame eggs. He wants us to pay the full price — a whole fifty silvers — for these chickens he imagines he would have!" Keros' frown deepened. "There is more to this story, is there not?" "Well, the restaurant owner has now gone to the magistrate and lodged a complaint against us. The trial is in two days — and we can't pay that much! We'll be thrown in prison!" "This will not happen," Keros told the young men. "Go to the courthouse, and register my name — Tau — as a witness. Say that I may be found at this address." And he gave it to them. "But you weren't there!" the men protested. "Little matter, do it anyway. If you're going to prison, what do you have to lose?" Swayed by the Trickster's reasoning, the two young men agreed. When the day of the trial dawned, they went before the magistrate and asked him to enter the name Keros had given as a witness. The magistrate was annoyed, but such a thing was within the bounds of Belharan law, and so he had to agree. The magistrate called once, his voice ringing about the courtroom, but there was no ragged catfolk. He called again, with little effect. Turning to his bailiff, the magistrate said, "It seems like this witness isn't here. Go to this address and bring this Tau to me. I've half a mind to charge him for contempt of court." The bailiff took a number of soldiers and arrived at the address, a small shack by the slums. "By order of the Emperor's Law, Tau, you are to come with us." "Go away!" Keros replied from within the shack. "I'm very, very busy!" The bailiff wasn't about to leave empty handed. Kicking down the door, he ordered his soldiers to seize Keros, and seize him they did, dragging the rag-clad catfolk by the arms out into the streets and to the courthouse. Keros complained each step of the way that he was busy, oh so busy! At last, they made it back before the magistrate and hurled Keros to the ground. "Why are you so late?" the magistrate demanded. Keros waved his hands in the air. "I told your soldiers, I was too busy!" "And what task is so important that you can't come to a court of law?" "Oh, honorable magistrate, tomorrow I must begin my planting. I am going to grow wheat, and as such I have to boil enough wheat to sow all my fields. It's a long and laborious process, and as such I've been busy since before dawn." "Preposterous! How can one expect boiled wheat to sprout!" "Then how," Keros said sternly, looking straight at the restaurant owner, "can one expect boiled eggs to hatch into chickens?" The case was thrown out. |Once, Keros was at archery practice with three of his students. The Trickster set up a straw target in the shape of a bird, setting it in the high branches of a tree. The first student came up to him, bowed, and said: "Master, I am ready to begin." "Very good," Keros replied. "Do you see the bird?" "I do, Master." "And do you see the branch?" "I do, Master." "And the leaves?" "I do, Master." So on it went, with the rest of the tree, then the hills, then the sky. At the end of this questioning, Keros simply shook his head and bade the first student return to the bench. Now it was time for the second student's turn, and he, too, answered the questions the same way. Once again, Keros shook his head and bade the student sit back down. Now it was the third and final student's turn. "Do you see the bird?" Keros asked. "No, Master. All I see is the bird's eye." Keros smiled. "Draw your bow. We shall see what you've learned." The third student loosed an arrow at the straw bird, and hit it right in the eye. |A man dies — one of those mundane yet unfortunate deaths, like a mine cave-in or an accident with the plow — and finds himself in a dense forest aflower with fine cherry blossoms. Sunlight filters down through the canopy, but there are no shadows; the trees are thick enough to be impassable, but floating blue flames hanging in the air mark out a path. Seeing little choice, the man follows the dancing flames and happens upon a glade in the forest. From the other side of the clearing, he sees someone approaching. It is the trickster god Keros, immediately apparent by his vulpine nature, nine tails, and the bow slung over his shoulder. As the Trickster comes closer, it becomes apparent he is heading for a chair and table which had not been noticed before, but seem to have always been there, as objects are in dreams. The deity sits and takes out a large scroll from under the table, unfurling it and poring over its contents. "Ah, yes, you have lived a middling life, I see. Not good, not bad, but more on the side of good with a heavy dose of self-centeredness than anything else," he says. "That is about average; to be honest, I'm not sure why you're falling under my jurisdiction, but things are what they are. You were of reasonable intelligence, so you and your ancestors did something right in previous incarnations. This means I can offer you a choice." The Trickster claps his hands, and two shoji screen doors appear in the air. Rolling up the scroll, Keros steps between the two of them, and gives the man a deep, respectful bow. "Allow us to begin with the first door. Behind this door lies an easy existence; your job will be to raise butterflies. You will have a large greenhouse, and each day you must collect leaves with eggs on them before placing them in incubation trays. Then, when they hatch into caterpillars, you must feed them leaves that you grow. When each caterpillar forms a chrysalis, you must relocate it to the hatching chamber and wait for the metamorphosis to be complete, then release the butterfly after its wings dry." "You will live in a grand, luxurious mansion. Your job will take about three hours a day. You will dine at a fine restaurant for two meals, plus takeaway for lunch. But, the butterflies you release will fly upward out of the greenhouse and into infinite empty space where they will be destroyed. You will watch the results of your labor vanish into meaningless nothingness before your eyes, every day." "Now, for the second door. You will live in a small stone hut on a medium-sized island with rocky soil. Here, you will labor in clearing the land and planting it with the only crop that grows on this island, cabbage. You will survive on cabbage and the meat of an occasional goat, if you can bring down one of the wild ones that range the island. It is a hard and grueling life." "On this island are deer who love cabbage. They will not take it of their own accord, but whatever you bring to them, they will eat. You will not be allowed to eat them, either. But you will be able to observe them and the effects of your care upon them." The man becomes aware of a sensation that through its contrast to what he had been experiencing, reveals the shift in sensations that has occurred after death. He has not felt alive, but upon this decision, he feels more like he did when he was alive: a kind of trepidation mixed with hope, a sensitivity like cold air across his skin coupled with the loveliest, most carefree night. And yet, this choice is hard. The answer is obvious, and at the same time, it is not. He likes fine restaurants and large houses. The void, however, that is the thing. He thinks hard and gets nowhere. As he gives up on the decision and on himself for being too useless to make the choice, a memory comes back to him. His first daughter, with her first doll, which some years later had become ripped. He had taken it and re-stuffed it carefully, then mended the rents with rough twine he kept in the storehouse out back. Then he gave it back to her, not having told her what he was going to do, and observed to his surprise a look of ineffable joy on her face. Keros is watching him. "I see that your decision is made," he says, giving the man another bow. "So it must be. Good luck, and perhaps I will see you again soon." |One warm spring morning, Keros is napping at his shrine, having transformed into a bestial fox and curled up into a tight little ball. However, his nap is interrupted by a loud crashing coming from the forest path, two sets of quick footfalls, and he perks his head up sleepily as two women come running up the forest path, headed directly for his shrine. Barely has he woken up before the first woman throws herself before the Trickster, dragging the second in tow behind her. "Oh Lord Keros, I am in dire need of your judgement on a matter of law!" Sleepy and grouchy, the Trickster eyes the two women. "Do I look like a magistrate to you? Get yourselves to a courthouse." "Oh no, Lord Keros. As a Living God, your wisdom is great, and surely your judgement will be truer than any mere mortal magistrate. Furthermore, the local magistrate has been summoned to the Emperor's court and will not be here for the better part of this month." Keros sighs at the attempt at flattery, resigns himself to the fact that his nap is ruined, and sits up on his haunches. "Fine, fine. What is your dispute? This should be obvious, but I suggest you do not attempt to deceive a living god, especially one such as me." The first woman is quick to reply. "Lord Keros, I accuse my neighbor of being a thief! I sell grilled fish from my home, and every morning I work hard to prepare my husband's catch for sale at market; a simple seasoning of oil and herbs over a charcoal grill. Imagine my shock when I found my neighbor stealing from it what was rightfully mine!" Keros glances at the second woman, still cowering a little from being in the god's presence and more than a little pale. "You haven't said anything yet, woman. Are you not going to defend yourself?" The second woman bows her head and speaks. "Lord Keros, it is true that my neighbor sells grilled fish for a living, and she prepares the grill every morning. My husband and I are poor folk, and cannot afford her wares, but while she grills the fish the most divine of aromas lingers in the air. We leave the window open, such that we may savour the scent of grilled fish while we have our simple breakfast. That's all." "And I clearly overheard her say that being able to enjoy the scent of grilled fish — which should be rightfully mine — was almost as good as eating it! Lord Keros, she is a thief!" Keros squeezes his eyes shut. He is not having a good day. The living god looks between the two women for a few seconds, then his gaze alights on the latter. "Do you have any money on you, woman?" "My Lord, my husband and I are poor —" "Two coins are all I require. Your neighbor is right — the scent of her grilled fish is rightfully hers, and she needs to be recompensed for her losses." The second woman bows her head, but dares not argue with the deity's judgement. She walks up and places two copper coins before Keros, who takes one in each of his forepaws and brings them together; the clink of metal against metal reverberates about the forest shrine. Once. Twice. Thrice. And then, the Trickster nods to the second woman. "Come. Take back your coins." The first woman looks bewildered. "But weren't you going to pay me, Lord Keros?" Keros swivels his stern gaze towards the first woman. "The appropriate price for the aroma of fish is the sound of money; you have been duly recompensed. Now, I suggest that you drop the matter, for am I not wise, and my judgement greater than that of any mere mortal?" ]
rows.translation: [rand|贾西拉的统治者苏丹自诩为这片土地上最聪明的人，他对此感到无比自豪。事实上，他的学识确实渊博，他常常邀请来自萨瓦拉各地的学者来回答那些连其他人都无法解答的问题。这样的举动，无疑让他能够尽情展示自己的智慧，同时让他人感到羞愧——这真是件无比有趣的事情啊！ “世界的中心在哪里？”苏丹会提出这个问题，然后当没有人能够回答时，他会哈哈大笑。当然，他自己其实也不知道答案，但因为他提出了这个问题，所有人都以为他知道答案——或者是因为他的地位太高，没有人敢提出不同的意见。他对自己的这个计谋感到非常满意，于是颁布了一项公告： “谁能告诉我世界的中心在哪里，就能得到贾西拉所有的财富。但如果你答错了，等待你的只有死亡。” 谁不想要一笔财富呢？然而，却很少有人愿意冒着被处死的危险去接受苏丹的挑战——直到有一天，一只穿着杂色黄衣服、身材瘦高的猫族来到了苏丹的宫殿。 “我愿意接受苏丹的挑战。”他说。 这是前所未有的举动，不久整个宫廷的人都聚集了过来，而那个穿着破烂的猫族也被带到了苏丹面前。 “那么，你愿意回答我的谜题吗？要知道，如果你的答案是错误的，死亡将会降临到你头上。” “这个我懂。” “很好。那么，世界的中心在哪里呢？” 那个陌生人在苏丹的宫廷前露出了狡黠的笑容，确保所有猫族的贵族们都能注意到他。“就在我的脚下啊。无论我走到哪里，它都会跟着我；我移动，世界的中心也随之移动。” “太疯狂了！”苏丹惊呼道。 “是吗？那么，哦，伟大的苏丹，如果我错了，您就把整个世界拿给我们来看，让我们一起验证吧。像我这样的卑微平民，肯定很容易就被证明是错的。” 苏丹嘟囔着，抱怨着。竟然有人看穿了他的把戏！但他绝对不会把一大笔财富送给一个衣衫褴褛的普通人！“那个谜语只是第一个。这里还有一个：天空中有多少颗星星？” “不多也不少。”那个陌生人平静地回答道。 “那根本不是个答案！”苏丹怒吼起来。 “不是吗？那么我们就一起登上天空，数数那些星星吧，哦，苏丹。只有到那时，我才能证明自己是错的。” “太荒谬了。”苏丹怒吼道。“不可能。好吧，流浪者，我最后问你一个问题：我的头上一共有多少根头发？” “和我尾巴上的毛一样多。”他回答道。 “错了！”苏丹惊呼着从他那镶嵌着宝石的宝座上跳了起来，似乎想要当场掐死那个陌生人。“那不对！” “啊，但在你能够确定这一点之前，哦，睿智的苏丹，你首先必须数一数你头发上的毛发数，以及我尾巴上的毛发数。” 苏丹受够了被这个无名之辈愚弄，尤其是在他的宫廷面前。当这些谣言在猫族贵族们中传开时，他知道这件事一定会扩散开来——而他对此无能为力。 不过，至少他可以让这个敢于如此羞辱他的陌生人受到应有的惩罚。 “卫兵！”苏丹喊道。“抓住这个白痴！” 然而，在任何人来得及触碰那个陌生人之前，他身上的破布突然脱落了，那个猫族立刻变成了一个狐狸般的英俊男子。当周围的人们发出惊呼声，许多人纷纷想要向凯罗斯跪拜时，诡计之神却走上前，对着这位猫族的统治者做了一个嘲讽的鞠躬。 “你自以为很聪明，哦苏丹，的确如此。但请永远记住，总有人比你更聪明。” 随着一声笑声，诡计之神从人们的视线中消失了，但事情并没有就此结束。后来，当苏丹检查他的国库时，发现贾西拉的所有财富都已经被洗劫一空，国库里空空如也。 |有一天，凯罗斯正安安静静地做着自己的事，他以自己最喜欢的装扮——一只穿着破旧衣服、毛色呈琥珀色的猫族——在首都的街道上漫步。突然，他看到有两个年轻人朝他的方向走来，从他们的表情来看，他们显然遇到了麻烦。 “怎么了？”诡计之神走上前，问道。“需要帮忙吗？” 两个年轻人互相交换了一声忧虑的叹息。其中一个人看了看他的同伴，后者点了点头。“我们陷入了极大的麻烦。十个月前，我们来到首都寻找工作。那时我们又累又饿，实在走不动了，于是就在一家餐馆停了下来。我们在那里每人点了两个鸡蛋，总共四个，都是煮熟后腌制的——但吃完之后，我们才发现自己已经身无分文了！让我们永远蒙羞的是，我们不得不不付钱就偷偷溜走了。” 诡计之神皱起了眉头。“就这样吗？那你就回去把欠的钱还上吧！” “正是我们这么做的！”第二个人惊叫道。“我们终于找到了工作，前几天我们回到了那家餐馆，想要把欠老板的那一枚铜币还给他——那是我们买鸡蛋时欠下的钱。我们向他讲述了我们的经历，表达了我们的歉意，也希望能弥补这个过错。” “对于四个鸡蛋来说，这个价格似乎挺合理的。”凯罗斯同意了。 “问题就在这里！老板根本不愿意接受它！” “哦？他是为了奖励你的诚实而这么做吗？” “恰恰相反！他声称，如果我们没有吃掉那些鸡蛋，它们就会变成小鸡。而这些小鸡会再下更多的蛋，这样一来，在这十个月里，他从那些鸡蛋里就能得到大约三十只小鸡。他现在要求我们为这些他想象中会存在的小鸡支付全额费用——整整五十枚银币！” 凯罗斯的眉头皱得更深了。“这件事背后肯定还有别的原因，对吧？” “嗯，餐厅老板现在已经去告发了我们，法官将在两天后开庭审理这个案子——而我们根本无力支付那么多的赔偿金！我们肯定会被关进监狱的！” “这种事是不会发生的。”凯罗斯对那些年轻人说道。“去法院，把我的名字——陶——登记为证人。告诉他们可以到这个地址来找我。”然后他把地址给了他们。 “但当时你并不在场啊！”两人抗议道。 “没什么大不了的，反正都要去做。如果因此进监狱，你又能失去什么呢？” 在那个狡猾之人的说服下，这两名年轻人同意了。当审判的日子到来时，他们来到法官面前，请求法官将凯罗斯作为证人列入名单。法官感到有些恼火，但这种请求确实符合贝尔哈兰的法律，因此他不得不同意。 法官大声呼唤了一次，他的声音在法庭上回荡，但却没有出现那个衣衫褴褛的猫族。他又叫了一次，仍然没有效果。于是，法官转向他的法警，说道“看来这个证人不在这里。去这个地址把那个叫陶的人带过来。我真想以藐视法庭的罪名起诉他。” 法警带着几名士兵来到了那个地址——贫民区旁的一间小棚屋。“根据皇帝法令的命令，陶，你必须跟我们一起来。” “走开！”凯罗斯从小屋里回应道。“我真的很忙！” 法警绝对不会空手而归。他一脚踹开大门，命令士兵们抓住凯罗斯，士兵们果然照做了，他们抓住这个衣衫褴褛的猫族，将他拖到了街上，然后带到了法庭。凯罗斯一路上都在抱怨自己非常非常忙！ 终于，他们在法官面前将凯罗斯推到了地上。 “你怎么会迟到呢？”法官要求如此。 凯罗斯在空气中挥了挥手。“我告诉过你们的士兵，我当时太忙了！” “那么，有什么任务是如此重要，以至于你无法出庭受审呢？” “哦，尊敬的法官，明天我必须开始播种了。我打算种植小麦，因此需要煮足够多的小麦种子来播种所有的田地。这个过程既漫长又费力，所以从天还没亮我就已经开始忙碌了。” “荒谬！怎么可能指望煮熟的麦粒还能发芽呢！” “那么，”凯罗斯严肃地说道，目光直视着餐厅老板。“难道有人会指望煮熟的鸡蛋能孵化出小鸡来吗？” 这个案件被驳回了。 |有一次，凯罗斯和他的三个学生一起进行射箭练习。那个爱搞恶作剧的家伙在树的高枝上挂了一个鸟形的稻草靶子。第一个学生走到他跟前，鞠了一躬，然后说道： “大师，我已经准备好了，可以开始了吗？” “非常好。”凯罗斯回答道。“你看到那只鸟了吗？” “是，主人。” “那么，你看到那根树枝了吗？” “遵命，主人。” “那些叶子呢？” “遵命，主人。” 就这样，接着是树的其他部分，然后是山丘，最后是天空。在这段问答结束后，凯罗斯只是摇了摇头，然后让第一个学生回到座位上。现在轮到第二个学生了，他也用同样的方式回答了问题。凯罗斯再次摇了摇头，让那个学生坐回去。 现在，轮到第三个，也是最后一个学生了。“你看到那只鸟了吗？”凯罗斯问道。 “不，主人。我只看到那只鸟的眼睛。” 凯罗斯笑了。“拉弓吧，让我们看看你学到了什么。” 第三个学生向那只草编鸟射出了一支箭，正好射中了它的眼睛。 |有一个人死了——死于那种平凡却又不幸的死亡方式，比如矿井坍塌或是使用犁具时发生的意外——然后他发现自己置身于一片开满美丽樱花的茂密森林之中。阳光透过树冠洒下来，但却没有形成任何阴影；这些树木长得太过茂密，根本无法通行，但空气中漂浮的蓝色火焰却为人们指出了前进的道路。迫于无奈，这个男人跟随那些跳跃的火焰，在森林中找到了一片空地。 从空地的另一边，他看到有人正在靠近。那是诡计之神凯罗斯——他的狐狸般的外表、九条尾巴以及肩上悬挂的弓，立刻让人认出了他的身份。当诡计之神逐渐靠近时，人们发现他正朝着一张椅子和一张桌子走去——这两件物品之前并未被注意到，但它们似乎一直就在那里，就像梦中的物品一样。那位神明坐下来，从桌子下面拿出一卷巨大的卷轴，展开它，开始仔细研读上面的文字。 “啊，原来如此，你过着一种平平无奇的生活。不算好，也不算坏，但总体来说还是偏好的那一面，只不过其中自私的因素占了很大比重。”他说。“这还算平均水平吧。说实话，我不太明白为什么你会归我的管辖范围，但事实就是如此。你的智力还算不错，所以你在前世一定做了一些正确的事情，你的祖先们也是如此。因此，我可以给你一个选择。” 诡计之神拍手示意，两扇障子门便凭空出现。凯罗斯卷起卷轴，从这两扇门之间穿过，然后向那位男子深深地鞠了一躬，表示尊敬。 “让我们先从第一扇门开始说起。这扇门后面是一份轻松的工作：你的任务就是饲养蝴蝶。你会拥有一个很大的温室，每天都需要采集那些带有虫卵的叶子，然后将它们放入孵化箱中。当幼虫孵化出来后，你需要用自己种植的叶子来喂养它们。当每只幼虫都结成蛹时，你就需要把它们转移到孵化室里，等待它们完成变态过程，等到翅膀干透后，再将蝴蝶放出来。” “你将居住在一座宏伟豪华的宅邸中。你的工作每天只需要大约三个小时。你会有两顿饭在高档餐厅享用，午餐还会外带。然而，你释放的那些蝴蝶会飞出温室，进入无边无际的虚空，在那里它们将会消失殆尽。每天，你都将亲眼看到自己辛勤劳动的成果在眼前化为无意义的虚无。” “现在，来看第二种选择。你将生活在一个土壤多石的中等大小的岛上，那里有一间小石屋。在这里，你需要辛勤劳作，开垦土地，并种植这种岛上唯一能生长的作物——卷心菜。你的食物将主要来自卷心菜，偶尔也能捕到一些野山羊，如果能够成功捕捉到它们的话。这样的生活十分艰辛且充满挑战。” “在这个岛上，生活着一些喜欢吃卷心菜的鹿。它们不会主动去吃卷心菜，但无论你给它们带来什么食物，它们都会吃。不过，你也不被允许吃这些鹿。不过，你可以观察它们，以及你的照顾对它们产生的影响。” 这个人开始注意到一种感觉，这种感觉与他之前所经历的一切形成了鲜明的对比，从而让他意识到死亡之后，自己的感官体验确实发生了变化。他之前从未真正感受到过“活着”的感觉，但在这个时刻，他突然觉得自己又恢复了生前的那种状态：一种既紧张又充满希望的情绪，一种如同冷空气掠过皮肤般的敏锐感觉，同时又伴随着最为美好、最为无忧无虑的夜晚氛围。然而，这个选择实在很难做出。答案看似显而易见，却又似乎并非如此。他喜欢高档餐厅和宽敞的住宅，然而，那片虚空才是关键所在。他苦思冥想，却始终找不到答案。 就在他开始放弃这个决定，也开始责怪自己太无能、无法做出选择的时候，一段回忆突然浮现在他的脑海中。他的第一个女儿，和她的第一个玩偶——几年后，那个玩偶已经破旧不堪了。他把它拿过来，仔细地重新塞满了填充物，然后用存放在后院仓库里的麻绳修补了那些破洞。然后他把玩偶还给了女儿，却没有告诉她自己做了这些事情。令他惊讶的是，他看到女儿脸上露出了难以形容的喜悦之情。 凯罗斯正在注视着他。“我看你已经做出了决定。”他说着，又向那个男人鞠了一躬。“果然如此。祝你好运，也许不久后我们还会再见面。” |一个温暖的春日早晨，凯罗斯变成了一只野狐狸，蜷缩在他的神龛旁小睡。然而，森林小路上突然传来的巨响和急促的脚步声打断了他的休息。他昏昏沉沉地抬起头，看到两个女人正沿着小路朝他的神龛方向奔来。还没等他完全清醒，第一个女人就已经扑到了那个“骗子”面前，还将第二个女人拽在了身后。 “哦，凯罗斯大人，我在一件法律问题上迫切需要您的裁决！” 困倦又脾气暴躁的捣蛋鬼盯着那两个女人。“你觉得我像法官吗？快去法院吧。” “哦不，凯罗斯大人。作为一位现世神祇，您的智慧无比高深，您的判断肯定比任何凡人的法官都要公正。更何况，当地的法官已经被召往皇帝的宫廷，这个月的大部分时间他都不会在这里。” 凯罗斯对这种奉承话感到无奈，只好认命，觉得自己的小憩已经泡汤了，于是便坐了起来。“好吧好吧，你们到底有什么争执？这应该很明显才对，但我建议你们不要试图欺骗一位现世神祇，尤其是像我这样的神明。” 第一位女性很快就回复了。“凯罗斯大人，我指控我的邻居是个小偷！我在家里卖烤鱼，每天早上都会认真地将我丈夫捕来的鱼进行处理，然后拿到市场上售卖——只需要在炭火烤架上加入一些油和香草作为调味料而已。当我发现我的邻居偷走了本该属于我的东西时，我简直惊呆了！” 凯罗斯瞥了瞥第二位女性，她仍然因为身处这位神明面前而有些畏缩，脸色也显得相当苍白。“你到现在还没说一句话，女人。难道你就不打算为自己辩护吗？” 第二位女性低下头，开口说道。“凯罗斯大人，的确，我的邻居以售卖烤鱼为生，她每天早上都会准备烤架。我和我丈夫都是穷人，买不起她的食物，但每当她烤鱼的时候，空气中就会弥漫着那种极其美妙的香气。我们会把窗户打开，这样在吃简单的早餐时就能享受到烤鱼的香味。就是这么简单。” “我清楚地听到她说过，能够闻到烤鱼的味道——那本来应该是我的享受——就已经让人感觉几乎像真正吃到了鱼一样美味了！凯罗斯大人，她简直就是个小偷！” 凯罗斯紧闭双眼，今天他实在过得很不顺心。这位现世神祇在两位女性之间扫视了几秒钟，最终将目光停在了后一位身上。 “女人，你身上带钱吗？” “大人，我和我的丈夫都很穷……” “我只需要两枚硬币而已。你的邻居说得对——她烤鱼的香味确实属于她，她应该得到相应的补偿来弥补自己的损失。” 第二位女子低下了头，但她不敢质疑神的裁决。她走上前，在凯罗斯面前放了两枚铜币。凯罗斯用他的前爪各抓起一枚硬币，然后将它们碰在了一起；金属相互碰撞发出的声响在森林中的神殿里回荡。 一次。两次。三次。然后，那个狡猾的角色向第二位女子点了点头。 “过来，把你的硬币拿回去吧。” 第一位女性看起来显得十分困惑。“但是您不是说要付我钱的吗，凯罗斯大人？” 凯罗斯将目光转向了第一位女性。“对于鱼香而言，恰当的价钱就是金钱的声响；你已经得到了应有的回报。现在，我建议你放弃这件事吧，因为我不正是智慧的象征吗？我的判断力，难道还比不上任何一个凡人吗？” ]
rows.raw: ' [rand|The Sultan, ruler of Jassira, was proud and thought himself the cleverest man in the realm. It was true that he was extremely learned, and a man such as he enjoyed calling scholars from all over Savarra to ask them questions none could answer. What fun it was to flaunt his wit and shame others as he did! "Where is the center of the world?" the Sultan would ask, and then laugh when none could reply. Of course, he himself did not know the answer, but by his asking of the question, everyone assumed that he knew it — or was too cowed by his station to suggest otherwise. So happy was he with his scheme that he issued a proclamation: "The one who can tell me where the center of the world is shall receive all the wealth of Jassira. However, answer wrongly and you will receive only death." Who didn't want a fortune? Yet few were willing to risk execution to meet the Sultan's challenge — up until the day a strange, spindly catfolk dressed in motley yellow came up to the Sultan's palace. "I wish to meet the Sultan's challenge," he said. This was something which none had dared before, and soon the entire court had gathered while the catfolk was brought in his rags before the Sultan. "So, you wish to answer my riddle? Know that if your answer is wrong, then death awaits you." "I know this." "Very well. Where is the center of the world?" The stranger gave a sly grin before the Sultan's court, making sure all the noble lords and ladies of the catfolk had their eyes on him. "Why, right under my feet. It goes wherever I go, oh Sultan; as I move, so does the center of the world." "That's insane!" the Sultan exclaimed. "Is it? Well, oh great Sultan, if I'm wrong, bring us the world and we shall measure it together. Surely a lowly commoner like me can be easily proven wrong." The Sultan sputtered, the Sultan grumbled. Here was someone who had called his bluff! Yet he was not about to give a fortune to a mere man in rags! "That riddle was just the first. Here is another one: how many stars are in the sky?" "Neither too many nor too few," the stranger answered calmly. "That's not an answer!" the Sultan roared. "It's not? Then we shall go up together to the heavens and count the stars, oh Sultan. Then and only then may I be proven wrong." "Ridiculous," the sultan snarled. "Impossible. Very well, vagabond, I lay before you a final question: how many hairs are there on my head?" "As many as there are on my tail," came the reply. "Wrong!" the Sultan cried, leaping up from his jewelled throne and making as if to strangle the stranger where he stood. "That is wrong!" "Ah, but before you can be sure of that, oh wise Sultan, you must first count the hairs on both your hair and on my tail." The Sultan had enough of being made a fool of by this no-name stranger, doubly so in front of his court. With the whispers running through the lords and ladies of the catfolk, he knew that the story would spread — and there was nothing he could do to contain it. But at least he could make an example of this stranger who had dared to shame him this way. "Guards!" the Sultan cried. "Seize this cretin!" Before anyone could lay a hand on the stranger, though, the rags fell away from his body, and the catfolk was now a very vulpine and handsome man. As gasps ran through the court and many sought to prostrate themselves before Keros, the Trickster stepped up to the Sultan and gave the lord of the catfolk a mocking bow. "You think yourself clever, oh Sultan, and indeed you are so. But always remember that there are always those more clever than you." With a laugh, the Trickster vanished from sight, but that was not the last of it. When the Sultan later checked on his treasury, it had been utterly and completely emptied of all the wealth of Jassira. |Keros was minding his own peaceful business one day, walking through the streets of the capital in his favorite guise of an amber-furred catfolk in rags. Suddenly he saw two young men coming his way, and it was clear from their face they were in trouble. "What's wrong?" the Trickster asked, going up to them. "Can I help you?" The young men exchanged worried sighs. One of them looked at his companion, who nodded. "We are in terrible trouble. You see, ten months ago we came to the capital to find work. We were tired and hungry, so much so that we could not go any further, and so we stopped in a restaurant. There we ordered two eggs for each of us, a total of four boiled and pickled ones — but after we had eaten, we discovered we had no money left! To our eternal shame, we were forced to sneak out without paying." The Trickster frowned. "Is that it? Then go back and pay what you owe!" "That's what we did!" the second man exclaimed. "We finally managed to find work, and just the other day we returned to the restaurant and tried to pay the owner the single copper piece we owed him for the eggs. We told him our story, confessed our shame, and wished to make amends." "That sounds like a fair price for four eggs," Keros agreed. "That's the problem! The owner would not take it!" "Oh? Was he rewarding you for your honesty?" "Just the opposite! He claimed that if we'd not eaten the eggs, they'd have become chickens. Those chickens would have laid more eggs, and in these ten months he'd have perhaps thirty or so chickens from those selfsame eggs. He wants us to pay the full price — a whole fifty silvers — for these chickens he imagines he would have!" Keros' frown deepened. "There is more to this story, is there not?" "Well, the restaurant owner has now gone to the magistrate and lodged a complaint against us. The trial is in two days — and we can't pay that much! We'll be thrown in prison!" "This will not happen," Keros told the young men. "Go to the courthouse, and register my name — Tau — as a witness. Say that I may be found at this address." And he gave it to them. "But you weren't there!" the men protested. "Little matter, do it anyway. If you're going to prison, what do you have to lose?" Swayed by the Trickster's reasoning, the two young men agreed. When the day of the trial dawned, they went before the magistrate and asked him to enter the name Keros had given as a witness. The magistrate was annoyed, but such a thing was within the bounds of Belharan law, and so he had to agree. The magistrate called once, his voice ringing about the courtroom, but there was no ragged catfolk. He called again, with little effect. Turning to his bailiff, the magistrate said, "It seems like this witness isn't here. Go to this address and bring this Tau to me. I've half a mind to charge him for contempt of court." The bailiff took a number of soldiers and arrived at the address, a small shack by the slums. "By order of the Emperor's Law, Tau, you are to come with us." "Go away!" Keros replied from within the shack. "I'm very, very busy!" The bailiff wasn't about to leave empty handed. Kicking down the door, he ordered his soldiers to seize Keros, and seize him they did, dragging the rag-clad catfolk by the arms out into the streets and to the courthouse. Keros complained each step of the way that he was busy, oh so busy! At last, they made it back before the magistrate and hurled Keros to the ground. "Why are you so late?" the magistrate demanded. Keros waved his hands in the air. "I told your soldiers, I was too busy!" "And what task is so important that you can't come to a court of law?" "Oh, honorable magistrate, tomorrow I must begin my planting. I am going to grow wheat, and as such I have to boil enough wheat to sow all my fields. It's a long and laborious process, and as such I've been busy since before dawn." "Preposterous! How can one expect boiled wheat to sprout!" "Then how," Keros said sternly, looking straight at the restaurant owner, "can one expect boiled eggs to hatch into chickens?" The case was thrown out. |Once, Keros was at archery practice with three of his students. The Trickster set up a straw target in the shape of a bird, setting it in the high branches of a tree. The first student came up to him, bowed, and said: "Master, I am ready to begin." "Very good," Keros replied. "Do you see the bird?" "I do, Master." "And do you see the branch?" "I do, Master." "And the leaves?" "I do, Master." So on it went, with the rest of the tree, then the hills, then the sky. At the end of this questioning, Keros simply shook his head and bade the first student return to the bench. Now it was time for the second student's turn, and he, too, answered the questions the same way. Once again, Keros shook his head and bade the student sit back down. Now it was the third and final student's turn. "Do you see the bird?" Keros asked. "No, Master. All I see is the bird's eye." Keros smiled. "Draw your bow. We shall see what you've learned." The third student loosed an arrow at the straw bird, and hit it right in the eye. |A man dies — one of those mundane yet unfortunate deaths, like a mine cave-in or an accident with the plow — and finds himself in a dense forest aflower with fine cherry blossoms. Sunlight filters down through the canopy, but there are no shadows; the trees are thick enough to be impassable, but floating blue flames hanging in the air mark out a path. Seeing little choice, the man follows the dancing flames and happens upon a glade in the forest. From the other side of the clearing, he sees someone approaching. It is the trickster god Keros, immediately apparent by his vulpine nature, nine tails, and the bow slung over his shoulder. As the Trickster comes closer, it becomes apparent he is heading for a chair and table which had not been noticed before, but seem to have always been there, as objects are in dreams. The deity sits and takes out a large scroll from under the table, unfurling it and poring over its contents. "Ah, yes, you have lived a middling life, I see. Not good, not bad, but more on the side of good with a heavy dose of self-centeredness than anything else," he says. "That is about average; to be honest, I'm not sure why you're falling under my jurisdiction, but things are what they are. You were of reasonable intelligence, so you and your ancestors did something right in previous incarnations. This means I can offer you a choice." The Trickster claps his hands, and two shoji screen doors appear in the air. Rolling up the scroll, Keros steps between the two of them, and gives the man a deep, respectful bow. "Allow us to begin with the first door. Behind this door lies an easy existence; your job will be to raise butterflies. You will have a large greenhouse, and each day you must collect leaves with eggs on them before placing them in incubation trays. Then, when they hatch into caterpillars, you must feed them leaves that you grow. When each caterpillar forms a chrysalis, you must relocate it to the hatching chamber and wait for the metamorphosis to be complete, then release the butterfly after its wings dry." "You will live in a grand, luxurious mansion. Your job will take about three hours a day. You will dine at a fine restaurant for two meals, plus takeaway for lunch. But, the butterflies you release will fly upward out of the greenhouse and into infinite empty space where they will be destroyed. You will watch the results of your labor vanish into meaningless nothingness before your eyes, every day." "Now, for the second door. You will live in a small stone hut on a medium-sized island with rocky soil. Here, you will labor in clearing the land and planting it with the only crop that grows on this island, cabbage. You will survive on cabbage and the meat of an occasional goat, if you can bring down one of the wild ones that range the island. It is a hard and grueling life." "On this island are deer who love cabbage. They will not take it of their own accord, but whatever you bring to them, they will eat. You will not be allowed to eat them, either. But you will be able to observe them and the effects of your care upon them." The man becomes aware of a sensation that through its contrast to what he had been experiencing, reveals the shift in sensations that has occurred after death. He has not felt alive, but upon this decision, he feels more like he did when he was alive: a kind of trepidation mixed with hope, a sensitivity like cold air across his skin coupled with the loveliest, most carefree night. And yet, this choice is hard. The answer is obvious, and at the same time, it is not. He likes fine restaurants and large houses. The void, however, that is the thing. He thinks hard and gets nowhere. As he gives up on the decision and on himself for being too useless to make the choice, a memory comes back to him. His first daughter, with her first doll, which some years later had become ripped. He had taken it and re-stuffed it carefully, then mended the rents with rough twine he kept in the storehouse out back. Then he gave it back to her, not having told her what he was going to do, and observed to his surprise a look of ineffable joy on her face. Keros is watching him. "I see that your decision is made," he says, giving the man another bow. "So it must be. Good luck, and perhaps I will see you again soon." |One warm spring morning, Keros is napping at his shrine, having transformed into a bestial fox and curled up into a tight little ball. Barely has he woken up before the first woman throws herself before the Trickster, dragging the second in tow behind her. "Oh Lord Keros, I am in dire need of your judgement on a matter of law!" Sleepy and grouchy, the Trickster eyes the two women. "Do I look like a magistrate to you? Get yourselves to a courthouse." "Oh no, Lord Keros. As a Living God, your wisdom is great, and surely your judgement will be truer than any mere mortal magistrate. Furthermore, the local magistrate has been summoned to the Emperor's court and will not be here for the better part of this month." Keros sighs at the attempt at flattery, resigns himself to the fact that his nap is ruined, and sits up on his haunches. "Fine, fine. What is your dispute? This should be obvious, but I suggest you do not attempt to deceive a living god, especially one such as me." The first woman is quick to reply. "Lord Keros, I accuse my neighbor of being a thief! I sell grilled fish from my home, and every morning I work hard to prepare my husband's catch for sale at market; a simple seasoning of oil and herbs over a charcoal grill. Imagine my shock when I found my neighbor stealing from it what was rightfully mine!" Keros glances at the second woman, still cowering a little from being in the god's presence and more than a little pale. "You haven't said anything yet, woman. Are you not going to defend yourself?" The second woman bows her head and speaks. "Lord Keros, it is true that my neighbor sells grilled fish for a living, and she prepares the grill every morning. My husband and I are poor folk, and cannot afford her wares, but while she grills the fish the most divine of aromas lingers in the air. We leave the window open, such that we may savour the scent of grilled fish while we have our simple breakfast. That's all." "And I clearly overheard her say that being able to enjoy the scent of grilled fish — which should be rightfully mine — was almost as good as eating it! Lord Keros, she is a thief!" Keros squeezes his eyes shut. He is not having a good day. The living god looks between the two women for a few seconds, then his gaze alights on the latter. "Do you have any money on you, woman?" "My Lord, my husband and I are poor —" "Two coins are all I require. Your neighbor is right — the scent of her grilled fish is rightfully hers, and she needs to be recompensed for her losses." The second woman bows her head, but dares not argue with the deity's judgement. She walks up and places two copper coins before Keros, who takes one in each of his forepaws and brings them together; the clink of metal against metal reverberates about the forest shrine. Once. Twice. Thrice. And then, the Trickster nods to the second woman. "Come. Take back your coins." The first woman looks bewildered. "But weren't you going to pay me, Lord Keros?" Keros swivels his stern gaze towards the first woman. "The appropriate price for the aroma of fish is the sound of money; you have been duly recompensed. Now, I suggest that you drop the matter, for am I not wise, and my judgement greater than that of any mere mortal?" ]'
